transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-30
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Carter (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Mills (Cascade CTO), Priya Verma (Lead ML Eng), Sam Ortiz (PM)

Summary:
Redwood did a product walkthrough focused on structured output (JSON mode), function/tool calling, and guardrails. Showed API and Console flows, demoed schema enforcement, error handling, and a short live example extracting product attributes into a strict JSON schema. Discussed security (SOC2, VPC, KMS), performance tradeoffs (latency vs batching/quantization), and suggested next steps: send guardrails doc, demo notebook, run a small benchmark on customer's product catalog.

Topics covered:
- Overview of Redwood JSON mode & structured output
- Defining schemas and validation/guardrails in the Console
- Function/tool calling patterns and examples (order extraction, product lookup)
- Error handling and fallback model variants
- Security/compliance (SOC2, SSO, KMS, audit logs)
- Benchmarks and pilot next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Carter: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll give a quick 30 to 40 minute walkthrough today on structured output and function calling in Redwood, hope that's still good?
[00:12] Jordan Mills: yeah that's great, we've got about 40 minutes, thanks alex.
[00:18] Maya Patel: cool, I'll share my screen in a second, just to show the Console examples and an API snippet, there may be a bit of lag, sorry in advance.
[00:30] Sam Ortiz: quick note from our side, primary use case is ingesting product descriptions + attributes from merchant feeds, want canonical JSON for our downstream product search and recommendations.
[00:44] Priya Verma: and we have noisy input from partners, so schema enforcement is big; also latency requirement for inline edits is <300ms p50 ideally.
[00:58] Alex Carter: got it. so two lanes: realtime inline edits where latency matters, and bulk enrichment where throughput/cost matters, we'll show guardrails that help both.
[01:12] Maya Patel: ok sharing screen now -> Console -> Structured Output tab -> JSON mode. you can define a schema, required fields, types, enums. here's an example schema for product: { name, sku, price, currency, category, attributes: [{key, value}] } - (note: schema example is paraphrased in transcript)
[01:40] Jordan Mills: can you force the model to return exactly this shape? even if it hallucinates extra fields or omits?
[01:50] Maya Patel: great question. yes, we use a combo of prompt conditioning, static validation, and optional post-call strict parser. There are two modes: soft enforcement (we'll coerce into shape) and hard enforcement where we reject responses that don't match and trigger a fallback.
[02:06] Alex Carter: and we also support function/tool calling for deterministic steps — so if the model says call product_lookup, we route that to your product service or a Redwood-hosted function.
[02:20] Priya Verma: about errors — if strict enforcement rejects, what does the API return? is it a 4xx or 2xx with error field?
[02:28] Maya Patel: currently we return 200 with an errors array when you're in soft/coerce mode, and in strict mode we return a structured error payload plus a schema_mismatch flag; in the Console you can set retries or fallback to a cheaper model.
[02:45] Sam Ortiz: does that impact billing if retries happen?
[02:49] Alex Carter: yes retries and fallback calls count towards tokens; we show token-level cost in Console and you can set automatic retry limits to control spend.
[03:02] Jordan Mills: latency wise, what's realistic for strict validation + fallback?
[03:06] Maya Patel: for small schemas and short contexts, strict mode adds about 30-80ms on average for validation, plus any extra model calls if you retry; batching and quantized models help for high throughput pipelines.
[03:20] Priya Verma: you mentioned KV cache earlier — will that work across model variants?
[03:25] Maya Patel: yes, the KV cache works per model family and we have smart routing to ensure compatible variants are used when falling back, although for strict schema enforcement we recommend pinning to compatible variants.
[03:40] Alex Carter: ok let's do a short live demo — Maya take it away.
[03:45] Maya Patel: switching to API quickstart, here's a curl example for /v1/generate with output_format: json and schema_id: prod_schema_2026_05
[04:00] Maya Patel: (reads) payload: prompt: 'Extract product fields from raw description', schema: prod_schema_2026_05, mode: strict, function_calls: [product_lookup] - again paraphrasing for transcript
[04:16] Maya Patel: sending request... response - oh there's a minor mismatch, model returned string for price, strict mode flagged it, Console highlights the error and suggests coercion to float.
[04:32] Alex Carter: that's actually useful because you can see the guardrail catching the issue before it hits your downstream.
[04:38] Jordan Mills: if we want to run a pilot, we want automatic coercion for historical data, but strict mode for live edits. doable?
[04:47] Alex Carter: absolutely, that's a common pattern. bulk jobs run in coerce mode, live editor in strict.
[04:53] Priya Verma: can we map enums? like category taxonomy to a controlled list?
[04:58] Maya Patel: yes enums and fuzzy mapping — we also provide a plug-in mapping function that calls your category service as a function call to resolve ambiguous categories.
[05:10] Sam Ortiz: any sample code for that?
[05:12] Maya Patel: yes, we'll share a notebook with examples for schema + function calling; it's in the repo link I dropped in chat.
[05:20] Jordan Mills: on security — how are keys managed if we use private deployment? KMS integration?
[05:26] Alex Carter: for Private deployments we support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM, RBAC, SAML SSO; for hosted we have KMS integrations and audit logs, SOC2-certified controls.
[05:40] Priya Verma: how about data residency? we need EU-only for a subset of merchants.
[05:45] Maya Patel: you can pin routing by region in Console, and we support on-prem or VPC deployment for stricter residency — we'll include a region/replication doc.
[05:55] Jordan Mills: ok good. cost question — if we run product_enrichment at scale, what's the best practices to reduce token costs while keeping quality?
[06:05] Alex Carter: use prefix caching for repeated contexts, batch small records together with our batching engine, and consider a quantized variant for bulk jobs — Redwood Optimize will give suggestions per workload.
[06:20] Priya Verma: and does structured output change when quantized models are used? any higher failure rate?
[06:26] Maya Patel: slight uptick in subtle hallucinations sometimes; our evaluation harness runs your prompts against candidate quantized models and reports schema pass rates so you can pick the best model/quantization profile.
[06:40] Sam Ortiz: can we do function chaining? like model extracts product id, call product_lookup, then enrich with inventory via another function?
[06:48] Maya Patel: yes function chaining supported — you can define ordered tool calls or allow the model to call in sequence; we also have guardrails to limit call depth and execution timeouts.
[07:05] Alex Carter: quick note — we share benchmarking spreadsheets and a small harness you can run locally to compare throughput/latency between hosted and dedicated. we'll attach that.
[07:18] Jordan Mills: what's the SLA on Dedicated?
[07:21] Alex Carter: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets, depending on committed capacity; we'll share the Dedicated SLA doc.
[07:30] Priya Verma: during demo, model sometimes returned extra commentary text outside JSON — how do you strip that?
[07:37] Maya Patel: we add a strict response wrapper and a post-processor that strips non-JSON tokens; if it's severe we can set the assistant to only emit JSON by using function calling or very strict system prompts. but again strict mode will reject anything outside schema.
[07:55] Sam Ortiz: are there any examples where the model deliberately returns a function call instead of inline JSON?
[08:02] Maya Patel: yes for multi-step ops it's often cleaner to return function calls, e.g., return {"call": "product_lookup", "args": {"sku": "123"}} and then the runtime executes product_lookup. that'll be in the notebook.
[08:18] Jordan Mills: for our infra team, they'd want to run private with VPC and use our internal product service as the function target. doable?
[08:26] Alex Carter: yes, in Private deployments you can register internal endpoints for function routing, with mTLS and IP allowlists.
[08:34] Priya Verma: any limits on function call payload size? our product objects are sometimes large.
[08:40] Maya Patel: payload size limits depend on your deployment and we recommend storing large blobs in object store and passing references; we can bump limits for Dedicated/Private on request.
[08:55] Sam Ortiz: uh quick aside, are you compatible with our existing event pipeline (Kafka)?
[09:00] Maya Patel: yes you can plug our outputs into Kafka or S3; many customers stream structured outputs to event buses for downstream processing.
[09:10] Jordan Mills: on monitoring, how do we trace a failing schema extraction back to the exact prompt and model version?
[09:17] Alex Carter: Console has per-request traces, model/version, token counts, and you can enable full request logs (retention configurable) for debugging and audits.
[09:30] Priya Verma: can those logs be exported to our SIEM?
[09:33] Maya Patel: yes, we support exporting audit logs to customer S3, BigQuery, or SIEM via webhook.
[09:42] Sam Ortiz: any known gotchas with multilingual product descriptions? we have partner feeds in DE/FR/ES.
[09:49] Maya Patel: models support many languages, but schema mapping sometimes needs language-specific rules; we recommend language detection step and then localized taxonomy mapping. our Optimize product can evaluate pass rates by language.
[10:05] Jordan Mills: ok we're getting close to time — let's recap and confirm next steps.
[10:10] Alex Carter: recap: Alex will send pricing and guardrails doc; Maya will share notebook, schema examples, and Postman collection; Cascade will provide sample product feeds and run benchmark; schedule technical deep-dive with infra.
[10:25] Priya Verma: sounds good. also our security lead wants SOC2 evidence and architecture diagram; Jordan will share contact.
[10:32] Alex Carter: we'll attach a SOC2 pack and architecture templates.
[10:40] Sam Ortiz: thanks everyone.
[10:42] Jordan Mills: thank you, bye.

References shared in chat: https://redwood.example.com/demo-notebook (notebook), https://redwood.example.com/security-pack (SOC2 + compliance), https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/spreadsheet (benchmark template)

End of transcript.

Post-meeting notes:
- Demo hit common customer concerns: schema enforcement, function routing, strict vs coerce modes, latency tradeoffs.
- Use-case fit: Cascade can start with a 2-week pilot on historical data (coerce mode) and a week of live editor testing (strict mode).
- Follow-ups: attach demo materials and schedule infra deep-dive.
